segments.text: Good morning, everyone. This is the committee meeting of the Georgia Public Service Commission
October the 1st, 2026. We'll change the order a little bit this morning and I'll first call
on Commissioner Johnson for telecommunications.
Thank you. Thank you, commissioners. Thank you, Chairman Shaw and Vice Chair McDonald for
allowing me to go first in case I need to get out a little bit earlier this morning.
So I appreciate that. We'll now open the telecommunications agenda. There are no items for consent, only
one for the regular agenda.
Good morning. Item R1 is docket number 44669, telecommunication relay service generic docket.
Hearing aid distribution program provider, consideration of staff's request for commission
approval to issue request for proposal for the hearing aid provider.
Are there any questions?
Okay. Okay. The RFP is issue pursuant to provision of OCGA, 46530. It charges the commission
with establishing, implementing, administering and promoting telecommunications equipment
distribution program and contracting for such program. The hearing aid provider will provide
equipment and services and outreach to low income adult and children who are hearing
impaired in Georgia. Staff recommends the following dates for the RFP. RFP issue electronically
October 6, 2026. Submission of written questions October 13, 2026. Proposals due November 2, 2026.
Optional presentation by offers November 6, 2026. The proposal will be awarded on December
1, 2026 and hearing aid provider will commence operations on June 1, 2027. I'll be happy
to answer any questions.
When was the last time we did a RFP for the service?
It's been about three years ago. It's a five-year contract. It's three years with the option
of a two-year extension.
Have there been any issues with the program or this provider in particular?
No, there hasn't been any issues with this provider in particular.
Any other questions? All right. Hearing none, it's on the agenda.
We'll be thinking about you today. Thank you. The Senators of Protection, Commissioner
Hovind.
Great. We'll call it over to the Facilities Protection Committee, item C-1, please.
Good morning, commissioners. Item C-1, consideration of commission approval of signed consent agreements
in resolution of the following guffa violations, that is A through L.
Questions or comments on item C-1. I hope that on the agenda, C-2, please.
C-2, consideration of staff recommendation, issue a rule nigh side for failing to address
a consent agreement in the following guffa cases, that is A through W.
Questions or comments on C-2? Hearing none, look at that on the agenda. I believe there
are no other items on the agenda, so we can conclude with still your protection.
Thank you.
Thank you, Commissioner. We'll go to Energy, Commissioner Wise.
Thank you, sir. C-1.
Good morning. C-1 is docket number.
Please tell me.
My name is Ruth Somoia.
Thank you.
You're welcome. C-1 is docket number 75042, marketplace below that, lot 1, 68, 57 to 61,
and 161 to 164, Carmen Forsyte County from Georgia Power Company to Suwan EMC.
Consideration of requests for transfer of retail electric service, supporting documents
have been reviewed and are in order. Staff recommends approval.
Thank you.
Good morning, commissioners. Item number C-2, docket number 45199, energy business marketing
LLC, petition for amendment of its natural gas marketer certificate of authority, consideration
of staff's recommendation. On July 21, 2026, NRG business marketing LLC filed a petition
to amend its interim natural gas marketer certificate of authority, GM 48. In the petition,
NRG business stated that it no longer provides natural gas service to residential customers
that all residential customers had either terminated their service or transferred to
another marketer. In August, 2026, staff confirmed that NRG business no longer serves residential
customers. Staff recommends approval of NRG business request to amend its interim certificate
of authority.
Item R-1 is docket numbers.
Item R-1 is docket number 44280, Georgia Power Company's 2022 rate case. Georgia Power Company's
request for approval of its nuclear upgrades tariff and consideration of staff's recommendation.
The NU-1 tariff is a voluntary program for large commercial and industrial customers adding
at least 100 MW of new load. These customers may subscribe to zero emission credits tied
to additional nuclear generation created through future upgrade projects. Participants pay an
upfront enrollment contribution and monthly subscription charges based on the number
of zero emission credits retired for them.
They do not receive physical nuclear energy, only the zero emissions energy attributes.
Subscription levels are limited to customers' actual load and agreements can extend up
to 25 years.
For subscribing customers, NU-1 offers a predictable way to meet zero emission or sustainability
goals. For all other customers, NU-1 reduces cost impacts because subscription revenues
help cover the cost of nuclear upgrades, which Georgia Power expects will reduce pressure
on base rates and improve system reliability.
Staff finds NU-1 reasonable, protective of non-participants and in the public interest.
Staff recommends the commission issue an order approving the NU-1 tariff contingent
on the approval of hatch unit 1 and 2 upgrade projects in dockets 56002 and 56003.
I'm happy to answer any questions. Thank you.
Thank you.
Thank you.
Thank you, commissioners.
Marty?
I've got a few questions here. I think that we'll see this in the backup, so I'm not
able to really answer some of these questions for myself.
Program enrollment contribution, is that like a payment in aid of, sorry, cash in aid of
construction or a payment made of construction basically to help defray upfront costs? Is
that what that program enrollment contribution would look like?
Some of these would be-
Basically.
Okay. And each one of these are basically, sorry, thank you, Ben.
Yeah.
Yeah.
This could, I could also wait until R2 for some of these questions.
Yeah. Do you want me to read R2 since it's all interrelated and then we can go over everything
all at once?
Let's do that.
Okay. Perfect. Thank you.
So item R2, very much related to item R1 is docket number 56002, Georgia Power Company's
2025 integrated resource plan and docket number 56003, Georgia Power Company's 2025 application
for certification, decertification amended demand side management plan. This is Georgia
Power Company's application for approval of the 2026 plan hatch one in two nuclear extended
power operates or EPUs. On December 21st, 2026 pursuant to the order adopting stipulation
in the IRP, Georgia Power submitted this application. The proposed plan will eventually
add 49 megawatts of additional capacity at the existing plan. Plan had new square units
and leverages carbon free energy, customer subscriptions and benefits from the inflation
reduction act for the benefit of all customers. The proposed DPU project results in increased
electrical power generation by increasing the thermal output of the reactors. The backup
memorandum provides more information on the accounting treatment of the program enrollment
contribution and zero emissions credit payments as discussed earlier, but yeah, the PCs end
up happening upfront and then the zero emissions credits are based on megawatt hours produced
at the plants. So the commission staff has reviewed the proposal, issued data requests
and met with the company on multiple occasions to pursue modifications and improvements
to this application prior to its filing. Staff recommends the commission approve the
plan hatch one and two nuclear operates conditioned on also approving the tariff. Again, would
you please introduce yourself to the exception of Tom Bond? Because I'm not the oldest commissioner
here, but I'm an old commission. So, thank you. Dr. Ben. Dr. Dutchman, right? Yes.
Okay. So you answered contribution and native construction. That's what the program enrollment
contribution is. Each one of these is going to be bespoke, right? These, we've got two
different, we've got a tariff that will apply to customers that may or may not roll. So
that'll be decided on a bespoke basis, right? There's no minimum percentage of program
enrollment contribution. I'm a little confused by the five. Yeah. So there's, as of this
point, there's only one customer that's going to enroll in this program and they'll
be making for both for them. And you want tariff, okay, for both hatch and vocal. Yeah,
that's the only, yeah. And I mean, it's been in the news, it's Google. Right. Okay. Now,
I saw that the, there's a value to the payments from the zero energy credits and then also
the extended power upgrades, right? Have you separated out the value streams there and looked
at what those two different values works. I saw that the upgrades are kind of less
than what we predicted. Yeah. So hopefully I'm answering this. So yeah, there's a, there's
a value for what the PEC payments will be. And that's trade secret, but it's, it's, you
probably have access to that. And then for the, for the zero emission credits, then that
is paid per megawatt hour. There's a price currently set also trade secret, but that
will be that subject to change under the tariff. So are you convinced then that there
are safeguards in place to make sure that all other customers that aren't able to subscribe
in this, so residential, small commercial, that they are going to be protected. Even
if they're delays, we don't see the zero emission credits maybe play out as expected. Now they're
safeguards in place. Yeah. So, so yeah, the, the zero emission credits will only be paid
for as they happen. So as megawatt hours or kilowatt hours are generated and then having
the upfront payments will certainly defray costs. And so long-term contract, right? Do
you see up to 25 years, but there is the ability to exit this at a time. So the
question is if that happens, this is one customer as you just mentioned. So who would
be left there? Are the benefits only come over time, right? So we have to just expect
this customer will stick around for a quarter century in order to capture. So a breakeven
point and all of this is going to be the spoke, right? It's one customer. So at some
point we will have paid off this investment. I don't know where that, I don't have the
answer to that question yet. So these are some of the things I'd like to dig into a little
bit more. This was only filed September 21st. So it's only been in our hands for a week
and a half. I think something of this magnitude definitely deserves a bit of scrutiny. Understood.
Thank you. Thank you. Morning. Good morning, commissioners. Steve Hewitt's in on behalf
of George Power. And first I want to thank staff for working with us on this. This
was several months in the making. Parties that go to the docket can see the number of
data requests, the detailed level of the data requests, the amount of information that they
asked and I also want to thank the team at George Power for the amount of information
that they were able to provide to staff. So a big thank you to getting this together.
To some of your questions, Commissioner Hubbard, and I think I can answer a bunch of them
and feel free to ask any others. But the upfront PEC contribution is a dollar value that is
negotiated with the customer and the participation agreement, right? That value alone brings significant
amount of significant amount of money to pay down the expenses of doing the project itself.
And then as Dr. Deutschman was talking about the ZEC, the zero emission credit payments,
are a stream of value that go out over 25 years for the participation agreement. But
one thing I want to point out is these upgrade projects, the Yates, or I'm sorry, the Vogel
upgrade project was approved in the 2025 IRP as economical without any contribution from
a customer. The Hatch upgrade projects similarly are economical without any value revenue coming
from another customer. The value that we get by doing the NU1 tariff and the participation
agreement brings literally hundreds of millions of dollars of value to the customers, to all
other customers. Combined with the energy benefits from the upgrades from nuclear energy,
between the four units that get upgraded, Georgia Power itself gets a total of about
100 megawatts, a little under 100 megawatts of additional value from these nuclear units.
The energy value alone from that going forward for the life of the units is hundreds of
millions of dollars. When you combine that with the program contribution payment and
the zero emission credit payment, you're talking about approximately $950 million of value
that's brought to all the other customers. So the program has been designed, staff has
ensured that there isn't any scenario under which, whether there's a delay in construction
or even if the customer decides not to participate after a certain number of years, which by the
way, there are protections for that in the participation agreement that you'll see,
even if that happens, which we don't expect to have happen, there are hundreds of
millions of dollars of values to all Georgia Power customers from doing these projects.
Steve, could this be considered parallel to accelerated depreciation
in far as for the customs benefit? Because we have that in over earnings and revenue caps.
Yeah, for sure. You're getting a little bit more into probably, I don't want to say anything wrong
because I'm not an accountant and somebody will tell me that I'm misinterpreting depreciation,
but what we're doing is we're increasing the amount of energy that you're getting from each
of the units and then that brings you back. Perhaps in retirement?
Still have to have the capability. Numbers are not my thing, Commissioner Wise, as you know.
But I wouldn't equate it to accelerated depreciation because you're increasing the output from the
units that you're getting and then that is providing that energy value to customers
for the remaining life of the units. So is it fair to say, just to kind of simplify things that
we approved these improvements last year? For Vogel. For you all to go out and
make these improvements to increase the amount of generation coming from these two older units.
And you all have gone out and found a customer to pay for it.
Yes, in essence.
Yeah, in the 2025 IRP, we proposed both the Vogel and the Hatch upgrade projects.
Staff supported the Vogel upgrade projects and said, let's wait on the Hatch projects.
And we said, okay, that was a stipulated settlement. And that's where we were
proceeding and we would have expected to bring the Hatch upgrade projects back in
2028 in the IRP. We continue to work with larger customers, multiple customers in terms of
generating additional lower carbon and carbon free energy. And this one with Vogel took to cold.
We actually talked to multiple customers about it, but as it has been identified,
Vogel is the one that ultimately signed on for this tariff. And we brought it back to staff and
essentially said, we've already approved Vogel. We would like to do Hatch and we have a customer
who is willing to contribute to pay down the cost so that those costs don't go on all other
customers. It is a massive benefit to bring to all customers to get hundreds of millions of dollars
to pay toward a project that already was economical and probably, I think, would have been
approved in the 2028 IRP because it was economical in 2025. It would have been
it's economical in 2028. Staff recognized the value of bringing this project to the commission
and to all customers and then the value that it brings to all our customers. And so we reached
an agreement. There were, like I said, months of discussions and meetings with them and staff had
some concerns that we worked through to make sure that we were coming to the commission
essentially jointly in agreement that this program as it's designed and the accounting treatments
that staff insisted on bring the maximum value to customers. Question for you. Is there an
opportunity for Georgia Power to file with staff follow a public pro forma agreement and a public
summary of material terms so that constituents and our customers understand what's happening
and that there will be no cost or overrun or recovery from them? Yes, a lot of that information
is included in the application itself, Commissioner Johnson, but there is no pro forma agreement,
but what we could do is, like the large load agreements, if you want, we could file a summary
of that participation agreement and the benefit that it brings to customers. Absolutely, we'd be
happy to do so because it is a huge tremendous benefit to all customers. Yeah, and in a way that
the public can understand. So that's a part of the transparency and accessibility. Yes,
Commissioner. Absolutely. Thank you. I guess what I want to fundamentally hear an answer to
is this nuclear upgrade is caused by one customer. Can I pause you there? It is not caused by one
customer. These were projects that were brought in the 2025 IRP by the company, and Vogel,
1 and 2 were approved. Hatch 1 and 2 are not approved. These were projects that Georgia
Power has been working on for years. We brought in the 2025 IRP. We got half of them approved.
The other half, we were told to wait until 2025. In talking to large load customers, they said,
is there a way for us to spur this on? So it was of Georgia Power's and Southern Nuclear's
idea to do the projects. Google has come in subsequent to us proposing them and said,
you didn't get approval for Hatch 1 and 2, but let us help you in terms of the economics
and make it even more beneficial for your customers, and that's what they've done.
Right. We've already litigated the 2025 IRP. I don't know if you looked at alternative
scenarios, low gas prices. The value of the avoided energy would be different in that scenario.
We're also basing this on an avoided CT, and I don't know that that's the best metric anymore
as well. Set that aside. The point is that the majority, if not the lion's share, 85% plus,
of this load growth is from data centers. So maybe don't ascribe it to one particular customer,
but this nuclear upgrade is needed for large load customers. So we have a ratepayer protection
pledge. What I want to hear from you is whether or not 100% of costs are fully covered by the
customers that are precipitating this need for a nuclear upgrade. Is there any cost shifting
onto non-subscribers? Are they covering 100% of the costs?
Of the actual upgrade? Yes.
I'd have to go back and look, I don't think it's fully 100% of it. But again, when you look at
the energy value that you get from the upgrades, you get 100 megawatts of carbon free energy
in addition to, and I understand your comparison to CCs versus CTs or other
sources of generation. But remember, these are nuclear megawatts. So they are some of the
absolute lowest cost. So anything that's generated from any resource above the nuclear cost
in terms of per megawatt hour is going to be a benefit of all customers. And combined with the
upfront payments, the value stream, and the energy benefits, you're talking about almost
a billion dollars of value to customers. So I can't say that 100% of the actual
construction costs are covered by the PEC or the ZEC credits. It's close. But regardless,
again, these were projects that were economic to do, regardless of whether there was a revenue
stream from a third party. So the revenue stream from the third party provides additional benefits
for customers and helps all other customers. That will play out over time. So they're not
covering 100% of the upfront construction costs. The benefits will be realized at the top.
Well, no, there are also benefits that you get from the upfront PEC payment that pays down those
costs. It's not quite a CIAC, but it's accounting wise, or not to a non-accountant, it's generally
the same. So you get that value upfront, but you also then do get the value stream over time as
you get not only the ZEC payments, but you also get the energy value from it. So it's both upfront
and it's over the life of the units. Last question, did the customer offer to pay
for 100% of the upfront capital costs for this upgrade? I wasn't in all the negotiations.
They were hurtful with that customer in terms of getting as much dollar value as we could out of
it. I don't think there was ever an offer for them to pay 100% of it, but the amount of money,
and you can see it in the trade secret backup, the amount of money that they are paying
is significant. Does their contribution make the system and the upgrades make the system
more reliable or less reliable? I would say it makes it absolutely more reliable. The more
generation you can get from our nuclear units, the better. Thank you.
If there's anything further, we'll include this item. Mr. Hubbard?
Okay. Item D1, what I'd like to bring forward for consideration, I'll give you some background.
This is a motion regarding utility deposit requirements. Georgia Power's current deposit
requirement structure presents a barrier for many residential customers, including those with low
credit scores or limited payment histories. The company may require residential customers to
pay a security deposit equal to up to two times the average monthly bill at the residence,
which for some could be 500 or more. For customers enrolled in the prepay program,
no deposit is required, but if they would like to go to a different tariff where there are other
options and programs available to them, they're not able to do that if they can't escape this
trap of having to be able to get past that upfront large lump sum payment.
There's also a lot of more disconnections with prepay customers, higher effective costs due to
transaction fees, and just fewer options for a rearage management or payment plans.
So this is a barrier. And what I would like to do is move the Georgia Power company be required
to offer residential customers the option to pay any assessed security deposit and 12 equal
monthly installments. Installment options shall be available to new customers and the customers
transitioning from the prepay program to traditional post-paid service. Customers
electing this option should not be required to pay the full deposit upfront. Additionally,
Georgia Power shall offer alternative forms of deposit satisfaction, such as third party
guarantees, letters of credit, automatic bank draft enrollment, etc. Consistent with the best
practice approaches used in other states. Furthermore, Georgia Power shall evaluate
options for deposit exemptions for low income customers. So there's a requirement here to offer
alternatives and then also to evaluate further options. In conclusion, these measures help ensure
that customers are not structurally trapped in the prepay program due to an inability to pay
large upfront deposits, while allowing Georgia Power to maintain adequate protections against
bad debt risk and cost shifting. That's the motion. Commissioners, Georgia Power,
Brandon Marzo on behalf of Georgia Power company. We recently received the motion,
so I'm going to give you our preliminary thoughts as it pertains to the motion
this morning. Let me start by saying that the company wants and I think consistent with the motion
customers be able to avail themselves of the rate options that are available to their rate glasses.
That's why we have a number of residential rates, several in fact more than the typical utility
because we do want customers to use and be able to be able to get on rate options. As the
commission is aware, requiring deposits, we talk about this, deposits and bad debt is
part of rate cases. Part of that is because when there's bad debt, that negatively impacts
all of our customers and ultimately negatively impacts rates. The reason we collect deposits
is to protect all customers. It's not to the benefit of the company, it's to benefit of keeping
rates as low as they potentially or possibly can be that it pertains to the impacts that
bad debt can have on rates. That's why we're doing deposits and ultimately under your
commission rule, we return those deposits to customers with interest if the payment history
is consistent for the 24 months that's required by the commission rule. I do want to clear up a
couple of things that I think are just not as maybe as clear in terms of what is the current
environment for deposits. We currently do require deposits when credit histories require it,
but our deposits are capped at $200. We don't charge more than $200 for deposits.
We've done some preliminary research on that once we got the motion yesterday. We believe that is
one of the lowest in the country and probably the lowest amongst our peers in terms of deposits.
We do offer installments. We don't offer 12 months of installments. We do offer two installments,
two installment payments to pay that deposit. That's the current state for in terms of how
we handle residential deposits. These are residential deposits. I want to be clear. We're
not talking about commercial and large businesses' deposits. I don't think your motion is either,
but that's how we're currently handling deposits. I want to point out the prepay where prepay,
as we talked about in the 2019 rate case, is a program that doesn't require a deposit.
It is an option for customers, just like our other rate options. It's there because there
are customers who are on the R rate at times who need to go to prepay because it does allow them
with arrears to be on the R rate. You can have arrears where in the R rate, you don't pay a bill.
At some point, you get disconnected. You can transition over prepay and you get a portion of
your prepay bill amount allocated to arrears. It's a safety net in many respects. To some
customers and to other customers, it's a beneficial management control option that they utilize.
It's a beneficial rate. I don't believe the motion is challenging the benefits of the rate,
but I do want to point out that the rate is used in a beneficial way by customers.
The last thing that I can say at this point, like I said, just having preliminary opportunity
to review the motion, is in terms of alternative deposit options, my concerns or the company's
concerns there would be really two-for-all. We're willing to talk about that, obviously,
with the commission if they want to explore that. With guarantees and letters of credit,
and you talk about the community that might be most impacted by needing to get
relief from a $200 deposit payment, I'd first be concerned that there'd be predatory practices
in place. Particularly letters of credit, when you think about what a letter of credit is to best
larger businesses, to get that sort of facility, and to monitor that sort of facility both takes
cost for the company, but also is cost for the customer. I'd be worried that a customer using that
type of facility would may pay more, well more than $200 to get it, and may be in a situation
where they're not dealing with the best entity to get that. In terms of guarantees, similar
situation, you don't know how that's particularly going to flow, so that'd have to be developed
and talked about, and dated have to be developed to figure out what is the best way to do
those sorts of things we wanted to do those sorts of things. In terms of direct deposits
or direct withdrawals, my only comment here is that in that, as that pertains to an alternative,
it's really not a deposit alternative. What that is, is that gives you the ability to know that
uncollectible is going to happen sooner, because you're able to draw on it. You don't have to wait
like our rate would have you wait several cycles potentially before you knew that you
weren't going to collect. You do find out you're not going to collect sooner, but you don't have
the backstop of the deposit. So you still don't have the money to apply, yes, whatever the usage
was, which is the intention of the deposit, which is essentially to protect customers from
uncollectibles that can occur, because we're basically giving credit when we allow usage
in advance of payment. So I sell that to say there's a lot of things to unwrap here.
We're not opposed to looking at options, even alternatives, particularly for the low-income
community that are outside of just sort of our normal practices as they stand. But we have done
several things that I don't know the Commission was aware of, like the $200 capital deposits,
like the installment payments that we think are fairly protective and working. But we're willing
to look at more things. But we do think we need to have time to look through that, have data.
And, you know, we do change an approach or add additional options that we have some
some good understanding of what those are, what the impacts and costs would be to customers.
I appreciate that additional color. And the idea behind the letter of credit is there's
an increasing pool of people that are suffering and having trouble paying their bills. This is
a way to, and I agree, we would have to have vetted institutional players, but there could be
banks and others that have been pre-vetted that help provide an umbrella letter of credit to a
certain number of folks. Something along those lines, I still think it's good to know that the max
deposit is capped at $200, spread over two different payments. That can still be a barrier.
And I think spreading it out over 12 months, there, you know, I'll have to see the data. And if you
have it, I'd love to see it on whether or not spreading out payments over a period of time
would actually impact bad debt payments. I think the two are quite fine.
The issue I find with your motion is the word require. I always thought that less government
was the best government that we could have. And I say that with the background that we
have here, dealing with the CWIP and plant Vogel. In the law that was passed by folks across the
street, initiating CWIP and the Vogel operation, it said shall collect. It didn't say may collect,
it said shall collect. That was a mandate. But when we went into the construction process
and plant Vogel, CWIP passed the legislature with the knowledge that it was going to be
so many dollars over a certain period of time. And we far exceeded both of those in time,
but we could not change the word shall at the commission. It would have had to been done
across the street. Now, what did that mean? It meant that all of us that are customers today
over the next few years are going to pay that interest cost. It's going to be downloaded all
with senior citizens, whatever it is, going to pay that company. When the process of the nuclear
generation is going to last for 80 years. So all these out through here, not going to have
to pay any of that, it's going to be dumped on everybody up front. The word require is a problem
for me. It doesn't give the company an opportunity to relook, to see innovation that comes along
as times change. The only requirement here is that they shall offer alternative forms of
deposit satisfaction. It's not prescriptive. It doesn't say what those alternatives need to be,
but an alternative beyond what we have here. Will you take the word may in lieu of?
May offer alternative forms. And so to require?
Doesn't that kind of negate the point of this? Not to make it done. Okay. Well, if this will allow
the opportunity to evaluate alternative forms and then the company will come back and provide their
evaluation of third party guarantees, other alternatives, then yes, I would entertain that.
And then we'll come back and fix it later on. I would like to find out a little more about what,
you know, let me, let me, let me do this, commissioner, and thank you for responding to
my request that you forwarded these discussion items to us in advance that we got to see that. But
what I'm hearing is that this is probably the best opportunity in light of just even the
differences between 500 and 200 is that we hold this item. So to hold it for 30 days
and have briefings back to the commission for these facts, these alternatives that we have
and any language changes that we might have. And so I'm just going to go ahead and hold this.
But thank you again for providing this in advance so that we have a better understanding
when we come into the committee. Thank you. I know the item is held, but I do want to just
on record indicate quickly that in review of the item, I'm mostly concerned about the predatory
issues and that could happen with this particular rate class and group of our constituents,
given that a lot of the banking protections that were once in place have all been rolled back
during our current federal administration. And there are a lot of banking issues, for example,
direct deposit if something's taken out and the accumulation of fees and all those things. So I
think there's a lot of things that surround this that should be included in that 30-day review.
And I'm baffled by the term predatory. I haven't heard that before. No, I'm saying if we were,
if folks were to seek out other ways or letters of credit or there could be predatory lenders
involved is what I'm suggesting. And then there could be overruns in bank accounts and things like that.
But we'll have an opportunity to flesh this out. And if you could explain that more to me in the
future, I'd appreciate that. That was the term that Mr. Marza used for that was his word.
Okay, we can move on to the second item. A quick background. This is a motion requiring
itemized residential billing. So each monthly bill here, I'll just start with the motion.
I've moved that the commission require Georgia Power Company to provide fully
itemized residential bills as the default billing format for all residential customers.
Each monthly bill shall separately identify the major components currently included within
the current service charge, including the non-limited to the basic service charge,
energy charges, and fuel cost recovery charges. All other charges for now shall remain itemized,
including the environmental compliance cost recovery, demand side management,
municipal franchise fee, sales tax, and any other commission approved charge, rider,
fee, or credit fund. Georgia Power already provides this itemized bill upon request.
So implementing this billing as the default does not require any new billing requirements
and it opposes minimal administrative burden. It is a minimal effort to
